references.text: The principle that one who sins without knowing it still bears guilt, but with milder consequences. [ref:Lev 5:17|Leviticus 5:17] describes the guilt offering for someone who sins unintentionally – parallel to the servant who acts wrongly without knowledge and receives fewer blows.

[ref:Num 15:27-29|Numbers 15:27-29] distinguishes between sin committed in ignorance and sin done deliberately, reflecting Jesus' teaching that the one who did not know his master's will receives a lighter punishment.
[ref:Deut 25:2-3|Deuteronomy 25:2-3] establishes that blows must correspond to the offense – a principle of proportional punishment underlying Jesus' words about few or many blows.

[ref:Lk 12:47|Luke 12:47] is the immediate context: the servant who knew his master's will but did not act accordingly receives many blows – in contrast to the one who did not know the will (v. 48) and receives fewer blows.
[ref:Jas 3:1|James 3:1] warns that teachers will receive a stricter judgment, confirming the principle that greater knowledge and responsibility lead to stricter evaluation.
[ref:Jn 9:41|John 9:41] – Jesus says that because the Pharisees claim to see, their sin remains. Greater knowledge brings greater responsibility, as Luke 12:48 teaches.
[ref:Jn 15:22|John 15:22] – Jesus says that if he had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin, but now they have no excuse. Knowledge of truth increases responsibility.

[ref:Rom 2:12-13|Romans 2:12-13] – Paul writes that those who sinned without the law will perish apart from the law, and those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law. The principle is that judgment is adjusted to the knowledge one has received.
[ref:1 Tim 1:13|1 Timothy 1:13] – Paul received mercy because he acted in ignorance and unbelief. An example showing that ignorance is a mitigating circumstance, as Jesus teaches in Luke 12:48.

[ref:Matt 25:14-30|Matthew 25:14-30] – The parable of the talents emphasizes that the one to whom much has been entrusted must give an account for much, and the one to whom little was entrusted, for little – "from everyone who has been given much, much will be required".
[ref:1 Cor 4:2|1 Corinthians 4:2] – Stewards are required to be faithful. Parallel to the principle that to whom much is entrusted, much will be required.

[ref:1 Pet 4:10|1 Peter 4:10] – Each should serve with the gift they have received, as good stewards of God's varied grace. Stewardship involves responsibility – from the one who has been given much, much is required.

[ref:Ezek 3:17-18|Ezekiel 3:17-18] – The watchman who has been entrusted with warning the people is held responsible if he does not do so. An illustration that great entrusted responsibility brings a great demand.

[ref:Amos 3:2|Amos 3:2] – "You only have I known among all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities." Israel received much and was held strictly accountable – an Old Testament expression of the principle in Luke 12:48.
